title: A Autopsy for the Letter
premise: Edmund Thornbury, an insurance investigator with a photographic memory, has spent two decades cataloguing the quiet town of Marrow's Bend and its secrets—until a drowned man is found wearing clothes stolen from Edmund's own closet, each garment tied to a claim file from thirty years ago. The victim is the son of a woman whose death Edmund once ruled accidental to protect the town's most powerful family, the Ashcombes. As Edmund reopens old files, every alibi he recorded begins to unravel, revealing that someone else remembers everything too—and has been arranging the evidence like letters in a filing cabinet addressed to him alone. In the end, Edmund must choose between exposing his own decades-old falsified report, which will destroy him, or letting the killer—the dead woman's other child, raised in exile—walk free; he chooses truth, testifying against himself as the heir surrenders, and the town's alphabetized silence finally burns.
about_author: Felix Ishikawa is the pen name of a former claims adjuster who spent eleven years reading other people's disasters before writing about them. They live near a lake that has never given up all of its dead.

chapters.title: The Filing Cabinet of Drowned Things
chapters.summary: Edmund Thornbury's POV. A body surfaces at Marrow's Bend reservoir wearing Edmund's own gray overcoat, monogrammed shirt, and lucky tie. Establishes Edmund's photographic memory and his obsessive archive of the town's claims, deaths, and secrets. Emotional beat: cold dread—the clothes are unmistakably his, yet he never reported them stolen.

chapters.title: Alphabetical Order of the Dead
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. Sheriff Dana Okafor asks Edmund to consult, since the victim—Paul Ashcombe—drowned on a policy Edmund underwrote. Edmund recognizes the staging instantly: items arranged A-to-Z by some private logic. Flashback seeds of thirty years ago surface unbidden. Beat: professional detachment cracking into personal fear.

chapters.title: What the Widow Kept
chapters.summary: Edmund interviews Vivian Ashcombe, matriarch, who greets him with unsettling familiarity: 'You wrote the letter, didn't you?' Edmund doesn't know what letter she means. Her son Paul had recently demanded access to his mother's sealed estate papers. Beat: the first hint that Edmund's own past work is the murder weapon's blueprint.

chapters.title: Claim No. 4471
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV, night office. He pulls his own 1994 file on Lena Ashcombe's drowning—Paul's mother—and finds his report flawless, too flawless, and one page missing: page nine, where his memory insists he wrote something he now cannot recall photographically. First time his memory has ever failed him. Beat: vertigo.

chapters.title: The Witness Who Wears My Socks
chapters.summary: Alternate POV: Ruth Calloway, retired schoolteacher, discovers her late husband's watch among the evidence photos. She admits someone has been leaving her gifts for months—objects she thought were memories playing tricks. She received a letter signed 'L.' Beat: dawning horror that the killer is courting the witnesses.

chapters.title: Thirty Years of Alibis
chapters.summary: Edmund reconstructs the night Lena died: four statements he took, four alibis he accepted without challenge because the town wanted it closed. He interviews each surviving alibi-giver—Vivian, her brother-in-law Gerald, the marina owner, and a young deputy since promoted to judge. Each alibi holds. Too perfectly. Beat: mounting suspicion that Edmund himself certified the lie.

chapters.title: A Letter for Every Lie
chapters.summary: Ruth's POV. A second letter arrives containing a photograph of page nine—blurred, legible only in fragments: 'I saw her go in. I said nothing.' Ruth brings it to Edmund, watching his face as he reads his own buried confession. Beat: betrayal—someone has been holding Edmund's guilt in escrow for thirty years.

chapters.title: The Heir Who Wasn't Filed
chapters.summary: Edmund digs into estate records and finds a gap: Lena had two children, but only Paul appears anywhere. The second child was removed from every record—by whom? Edmund's own archive contains a deletion order he doesn't remember signing. Beat: the realization that his memory may have been edited by his own hand.

chapters.title: Interrogation of a Photograph
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. Using his memory of the crime scene, he reconstructs what the staging means: the clothes spell out a sentence when ordered by their original claim numbers. It reads: 'YOU KNEW. SHE KNEW. NOW YOU KNOW.' The killer isn't hiding—they're corresponding. Beat: terror turning into grim resolve.

chapters.title: Gerald's Boathouse
chapters.summary: Edmund confronts Gerald Ashcombe, who breaks easily: he saw Vivian follow Lena to the water that night, took money to say otherwise, and has been paying blackmail ever since—to an account opened in 1994 under a name Edmund recognizes as an anagram. Beat: the alibis were purchased, and Edmund appraised them honestly anyway.

chapters.title: The Judge's Recusal
chapters.summary: Ruth's POV. The judge—one of Edmund's original witnesses—resigns abruptly and leaves town, mailing Edmund his own 1994 statement annotated in red: 'You never asked me where I was standing.' His vantage point would have shown him the second child on the dock. Beat: the machinery of protection beginning to eat itself.

chapters.title: Page Nine
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV, the novel's midpoint reversal. Under hypnosis-adjacent concentration, Edmund recovers why page nine vanished: he didn't hide it—Lena herself asked him to, dying words promising her children would be safer if the town believed an accident. He falsified the report as an act of mercy, then let his perfect memory bury it. Beat: grief; the price of survival made flesh.

chapters.title: Second Child, Third Letter
chapters.summary: Ruth receives a third letter: a birth certificate for 'Mira Ashcombe,' sent to a group home in 1995, signed out by a caseworker whose signature Edmund photographed long ago and can finally read. Mira lives forty miles away under another name, employed—impossibly—as an archivist. Beat: the hunter and the hunted share a profession.

chapters.title: The Archive of Mira Voss
chapters.summary: Edmund visits the county records annex and meets Mira Voss: calm, precise, surrounded by the same filing systems he uses. She neither denies nor confesses. 'You filed my mother under A for Accident,' she says. 'I'm just correcting your index.' Beat: recognition between two people who survived by organizing pain.

chapters.title: What Paul Found
chapters.summary: Mira's POV (unnamed narrator). Paul discovered her existence three months ago, blackmailed Vivian for money, and threatened to expose Edmund's false report to force the estate open. Mira confronted him at the reservoir intending only to frighten him; the drowning happened in a struggle she swears she didn't start—but she stayed to stage the scene as a message. Beat: unreliable confession, love and duty colliding.

chapters.title: Evidence Against the Investigator
chapters.summary: Sheriff Okafor's POV. Physical evidence turns: fibers from Edmund's closet in Paul's lungs timeline, Edmund's fingerprints on the staged garments. Okafor, who owes Edmund her career, arrests him anyway. Beat: duty over loyalty; the theme inverted onto its most sympathetic enforcer.

chapters.title: Twenty Years Invisible
chapters.summary: Edmund in custody, narrating from a cell. He reviews his life's ledger: every secret kept, every kindness bought with silence, including shielding Okafor's brother from a fraud charge years ago. He realizes invisibility was never safety—it was compounding interest on debt. Beat: reckoning; the price of survival itemized.

chapters.title: The Confession Letter
chapters.summary: Ruth's POV. Mira sends Ruth the final letter—her mother's actual last letter, hidden in the archive for thirty years—asking Ruth, the only adult who was kind to the children, to deliver it to Edmund. It confirms Lena chose the water knowing she was ill and insured, begging Edmund to let the accident stand so the payout would raise her kids. Beat: devastating tenderness; the mystery's moral core revealed.

chapters.title: Climax: Reading Aloud
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. At his bail hearing-turned-preliminary examination, Edmund takes the stand, reads page nine aloud from memory, and reconstructs the entire thirty-year architecture: Vivian's blackmail, Gerald's payment, the judge's silence, his own mercy-forged fraud, and Mira's staged scene. He names himself as the first liar in the chain. Beat: catharsis through exposure; love against duty resolved by choosing both—truth for Lena, protection for no one, including himself.

chapters.title: Sentencing
chapters.summary: Okafor's POV. Mira confesses fully to the staging and accepts manslaughter responsibility for the struggle; prosecutors, armed with Edmund's testimony, indict Vivian for the original cover-up conspiracy. Edmund pleads guilty to falsifying a report. Sentences land unevenly, as they always do. Beat: justice as imperfect arithmetic; inheritance paid in full.

chapters.title: Burning the Cabinet
chapters.summary: Edmund's final POV chapter. Released after serving his term's opening months, he burns his twenty-year archive of the town's secrets in a steel drum behind the office—except one folder, which he mails to Mira: everything about her mother, indexed properly, filed under L for Lena. Beat: release; memory kept human by choosing what to carry.

chapters.title: Epilogue: An Autopsy for the Letter
chapters.summary: Ruth's POV, one year later. Ruth and Mira correspond; the town pretends nothing happened, as towns do. On the anniversary, someone leaves flowers at the reservoir with a card bearing a single typed line: 'Filed correctly at last.' Edmund, passing on his morning walk, allows himself to forget—for one moment—exactly what it says. Beat: quiet peace; survival finally priced fairly.
